\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.

Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption; reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives, sacrificing recall; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime guarantees.
These two directions—grammar-constrained decoding and schema-aware training—have developed independently; no method provides both semantic awareness and runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.

Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
Recall the tightness of relation $r$ (\S\ref{sec:bg:ontology}):\footnote{For symmetric relations, $|\sigma(r)|$ counts ordered pairs; the normalization $|\mathcal{E}|^2$ remains appropriate since we evaluate on directed triples.}
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\sigma(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes schema restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
Recall the tightness of relation $r$ (\S\ref{sec:bg:ontology}):\footnote{For symmetric relations, $|\sigma(r)|$ counts ordered pairs; the normalization $|\mathcal{E}|^2$ remains appropriate since we evaluate on directed triples.}
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\sigma(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes schema restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate; $n{=}4$ model--dataset pairs, descriptive) aligns with the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
The pattern extends to WikiEvents EE ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.82$; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents-kappa}).
However, $\kappa$ is necessary but not sufficient for high violation rates: per-relation analysis shows that high-$\kappa$ relations with unambiguous entity types (\textsc{place\_of\_birth}, $\kappa{=}0.92$, DR${=}$0\%) have zero violations, while relations with comparable $\kappa$ but confusable types (\textsc{basin\_country}, $\kappa{=}0.97$, DR${=}$74.6\%) are highly vulnerable (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study}).
$\bar{\kappa}$ provides deployment guidance: schemas with $\bar{\kappa} < 0.5$ achieve near-complete DR elimination under zero-shot S1 (94--99\% reduction); schemas with $\bar{\kappa} > 0.8$ require fine-tuning to narrow the fallback regime (DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%).
$\bar{\kappa}$ also determines post-hoc resolution feasibility: low-$\bar{\kappa}$ schemas ($<$0.5) benefit from TCR with negligible DR regression ($\leq$0.28\,pp), while high-$\bar{\kappa}$ schemas ($>$0.8) suffer harmful DR increases (up to $+$9.38\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Greedy assignment limitation.}
\label{sec:greedy-limitation}
The semantic layer enforces type constraints greedily: each entity's type is committed at generation time and cannot be revised when subsequent relations impose conflicting requirements.
This is an instance of Level~3 (non-local) constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability})---global entity-type consensus depends on the full output and is undecidable at the prefix level.
CF violations arise from this greedy commitment: the same entity may receive different type assignments across triples, each individually valid but mutually inconsistent.
Post-hoc type consistency resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}) addresses this as a repair step rather than a generation-time guarantee; beam search resolves it by exploring multiple commitment paths simultaneously (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\paragraph{Fallback cascade analysis.}
Grammar-first fallback activates when semantic constraints leave no grammar-valid token ($S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$), relaxing to grammar-only selection.
Fallback frequency correlates with $\bar{\kappa}$: low-tightness schemas (SciERC, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) trigger fallback rarely, yielding 94\% DR reduction; high-tightness schemas (DocRED, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) trigger fallback more frequently, limiting DR reduction to 45\% under zero-shot.
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime by aligning model predictions with schema constraints, reducing fallback activation and achieving DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% across both schemas.

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.

% Appendix: Full Proof of Proposition 1
% Level 2 (prefix-decidable with state) constraints are not context-free.

\section{Full Proof of Proposition 1}
\label{app:pumping-lemma}

We prove that domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets cannot be expressed by any context-free grammar, using the pumping lemma for context-free languages.

\begin{proof}
Define the language $L$ of valid IE outputs over ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ with $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, $\mathcal{R} = \{r\}$, and $\sigma(r) = \{(\tau_A, \tau_A)\}$ (i.e., $r$ requires both head and tail to be type $\tau_A$).

An output string has the form:
\[
w = e_1\, e_2\, \cdots\, e_n\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_k,\, r,\, \tau^h)
\]
where each $e_i$ is an entity with type $\tau_{a_i} \in \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, and $\tau^h$ is the head type field of a relation triple referencing entity $e_k$ ($1 \leq k \leq n$).

The type-validity constraint requires $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k}$ (the head type must match the referenced entity's type) \emph{and} $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
Combined: a string $w \in L$ if and only if $\tau_{a_k} = \tau_A$.

Now consider strings of the specific form:
\[
w_n = \underbrace{\tau_B\; \tau_B\; \cdots\; \tau_B}_{n-1}\; \tau_A\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_n,\, r,\, \tau_A)
\]
where the first $n{-}1$ entities have type $\tau_B$ and only entity $e_n$ has type $\tau_A$.
The relation references $e_n$, so $\tau^h = \tau_A = \tau_{a_n}$, satisfying both the registry consistency and domain constraint.
Thus $w_n \in L$ for all $n$.

Assume for contradiction that $L$ is context-free.
By the pumping lemma, there exists a pumping length $p$ such that any $w \in L$ with $|w| \geq p$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ where:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $|vy| \geq 1$,
    \item $|vxy| \leq p$,
    \item $uv^i xy^i z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
\end{enumerate}

Choose $w = w_n$ with $n > p$.
The entity list portion $\tau_B^{n-1}\, \tau_A$ has length $n > p$, so the pumpable region $vxy$ (with $|vxy| \leq p$) must lie entirely within the entity list (it cannot span from the entity list to the relation reference, which is separated by $n - p > 0$ entity tokens from the start).

\textbf{Case 1:} $v$ or $y$ contains entity tokens from the $\tau_B^{n-1}$ prefix.
Pumping up ($i = 2$): $uv^2 xy^2 z$ inserts additional $\tau_B$ entities, increasing $n$ to some $n' > n$.
But the relation reference still points to entity $e_n$ (at the original position), which is now at a different position in the longer entity list.
The entity at position $n$ in the pumped string is $\tau_B$ (since we inserted $\tau_B$ tokens before position $n$, shifting $\tau_A$ to position $n' > n$).
Thus $\tau^h = \tau_A \neq \tau_B = \tau_{a_n'}$, where $n'$ is the new position of entity $e_n$.
More precisely: the relation references a fixed entity name $e_k$, but pumping changes the entity-type binding at that name's position.
Since the pumped string assigns $\tau_B$ at position $k$ (which originally had $\tau_A$), the type-validity constraint $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k} \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$ is violated.
Hence $uv^2 xy^2 z \notin L$, contradicting condition (iii).

\textbf{Case 2:} $v$ or $y$ contains the $\tau_A$ token at position $n$.
Pumping down ($i = 0$): $uxz$ removes the only $\tau_A$ entity.
The relation's head entity reference now points to a position that either does not exist or has type $\tau_B$.
In either case, $\tau^h = \tau_A \neq \tau_B$, violating type validity.
Hence $uxz \notin L$, contradicting condition (iii).

In both cases, the pumping lemma is violated, so $L$ is not context-free.
The key insight is that type-validity requires a \emph{binding} between an entity's type (assigned at an earlier position) and the relation's type field (at a later position), with the binding target determined by the entity name.
Pumping disrupts this binding by changing which entity occupies a given position, while the relation reference remains fixed---a cross-position dependency that pushdown automata cannot track with their LIFO stack discipline.

OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map), operating as a deterministic stateful transducer that provides random-access type lookups, beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.
\end{proof}
